beats.headline: Your code passes unit tests but fails in production?
beats.subline: Race conditions are silent killers. Here is why your bank balance is lying to you.
beats.narration: Your code passes every single-threaded unit test, yet in production, your bank balance drops below zero. This is a classic race condition, where thread interleaving destroys your business invariants.

beats.title: The Check-Then-Act Trap

steps.explanation: Two threads see the same balance and both pass the check.
Both threads subtract, leading to a negative balance.

beats.narration: The check-then-act pattern is dangerous. Two threads pass the balance check simultaneously, then both subtract the amount. The result is a corrupted state that violates your logic.

beats.title: The Race Condition Timeline
beats.subtitle: How interleaving kills data integrity
beats.narration: When threads interleave, they don't see each other's updates. Thread 1 and 2 both read the same initial state, bypass the safety check, and write back corrupted final values.

beats.title: Atomic vs. Non-Atomic
beats.narration: To fix this, we need atomicity. The synchronized block ensures only one thread executes the critical section at a time, forcing threads to queue up and wait their turn.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Race conditions occur in critical sections
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): How synchronized works under the hood →
beats.narration: That is the race condition. In Part 2, we look at how synchronized uses intrinsic monitors to lock objects and how the JVM optimizes these locks.

beats.headline: Why synchronize on a private final object?
beats.subline: Synchronizing on 'this' is a trap. Here is the right way to lock.
beats.narration: Synchronizing on 'this' is a common rookie mistake. External code can lock your instance, causing deadlocks. Let's see the safe way to manage intrinsic monitors.

beats.title: Safe Locking Pattern

steps.explanation: A private final object prevents external code from locking your instance.
Only one thread can hold this specific lock at a time.

beats.narration: Always use a private final object as your lock. This encapsulates the monitor, ensuring no outside class can interfere with your synchronization, preventing accidental contention or deadlocks.

beats.title: Bytecode: monitorenter/exit
beats.caption: How the JVM handles blocks
beats.narration: When you use a synchronized block, the compiler generates monitorenter and monitorexit instructions. The JVM ensures that even if an exception occurs, the lock is released.

beats.title: Reentrancy Explained
beats.subtitle: Threads don't deadlock themselves
beats.narration: Java locks are reentrant. If a thread already holds the lock, it can enter another synchronized block on the same object without blocking itself. The JVM simply increments a counter.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Use private final objects for locks
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Deadlocks, Livelocks, and Starvation →
beats.narration: That's how monitors work. In Part 3, we explore the dark side: how to identify and fix deadlocks, livelocks, and thread starvation.

beats.headline: Why do your threads stop making progress?
beats.subline: Deadlocks and livelocks are common. Here is how to break the cycle.
beats.narration: Your threads are running, but they aren't doing work. They are trapped in a deadlock or a livelock. Let's break the cycle.

beats.title: The Deadlock Cycle
beats.subtitle: Circular wait condition

nodes.label: Thread 1
nodes.detail: Holds Account A, waits for B

nodes.label: Thread 2
nodes.detail: Holds Account B, waits for A

beats.narration: Deadlocks occur when threads hold resources while waiting for others in a cycle. Thread 1 holds A and waits for B, while Thread 2 holds B and waits for A.

beats.title: Fixing Deadlocks with Ordering

steps.explanation: Always lock in the same order to break the circular wait.
This prevents the cycle that causes deadlocks.

beats.narration: The fix is simple: enforce a global lock order. By always locking the account with the lower ID first, you break the circular wait condition that makes deadlocks possible.

beats.title: Deadlock vs. Livelock
beats.narration: Livelocks are trickier. Threads are runnable and burning CPU, but they keep retrying in lockstep. Use randomized backoff to break the symmetry and let one thread proceed.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Use global ordering to prevent deadlocks
beats.narration: Deadlocks and livelocks are solved by ordering and randomness. In Part 4, we master thread signaling with wait and notify.

beats.headline: Why is your wait() call failing?
beats.subline: Spurious wakeups and missed signals are common. Here is the correct pattern.
beats.narration: Calling wait() without a loop is a bug. Spurious wakeups happen, and you must re-check your condition. Let's look at the correct signaling pattern.

beats.title: The Correct Signaling Pattern

steps.explanation: Always re-check the condition after waking up.
Atomically releases the lock and suspends the thread.

beats.narration: Always use a while loop. Wait can return due to spurious wakeups, and another thread might have grabbed the resource before you. The loop ensures your condition is still valid.

beats.title: Wait Set Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: How threads communicate
beats.narration: When a thread calls wait, it enters the wait set and releases the monitor. When notified, it moves to the entry queue to re-acquire the lock.

beats.title: notify() vs. notifyAll()
beats.narration: Prefer notifyAll. notify wakes one thread, but if it's the wrong type of thread, it goes back to sleep and the signal is lost. notifyAll ensures everyone checks the condition.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: Signaling is about robust condition checking. In Part 5, we wrap up with modern concurrency alternatives.

beats.headline: Why avoid synchronized in new code?
beats.subline: Java.util.concurrent offers better performance and more control.
beats.narration: Synchronized is fine, but Java's concurrent package is better. Let's see why you should prefer high-level abstractions over hand-rolled monitors.

beats.title: ReentrantLock vs. Synchronized

steps.explanation: Fair locks prevent starvation by using FIFO order.
Always unlock in a finally block to prevent leaks.

beats.narration: ReentrantLock gives you fairness options and tryLock capabilities. Always use a try-finally block to ensure the lock is released, even if your code throws an exception.

beats.title: Java Concurrency Toolkit
beats.subtitle: Beyond basic monitors
beats.narration: The java.util.concurrent package provides everything you need: atomic variables for lock-free updates, blocking queues for producer-consumer, and executors for managing thread lifecycles.

beats.title: Chapter Summary
beats.caption: Key Takeaways
beats.narration: We covered race conditions, deadlock prevention, signaling patterns, and modern concurrency. Use these tools to build robust, thread-safe applications.
